text: IOGP Life-Saving Rules Scope With the revision of Report 459, IOGP launches a simplified set of Life-Saving Rules to provide workers in the industry with the actions they can take to protect themselves and their colleagues from fatalities. IOGP aims to improve the level of industry-wide adoption across the global oil and gas industry. The reduced number of rules (nine) still cover a similar scope

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: reduced number of rules (nine) still cover a similar scope to that of the original 18 Life-Saving Rules: since 2008, 376 lives could have been potentially saved by following the revised IOGP Life-Saving Rules. IOGP Report 459 introduces the revised IOGP Life-Saving Rules, provides implementation guidance and the background data analysis. Additional implementation materials are available from https://www.iogp.org/life-savingrules.

section: 1. Foreword
text: 1. Foreword IOGP Member companies recognise the value of providing clear, simple, and consistent information regarding risks in the workplace and the proper use of barriers and safeguards to protect the workforce. In 2010 IOGP published a set of Life-Saving Rules to mitigate risk and reduce fatalities in the oil and gas industry. These were derived from analysis data reported to IOGP: 1484 fatal incidents

section: 1. Foreword
text: derived from analysis data reported to IOGP: 1484 fatal incidents (1991-2010) and 1173 high potential events (2000-2010). Following these simple rules could have prevented around 70% of these fatalities. While member companies and others benefit from implementing their own programmes, there is greater clarity and effectiveness to be gained in standardising Life-Saving Rules across the industry. Over

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: IOGP Life-Saving Rules 3. Implementing the Life-Saving Rules Standardisation of Life-Saving Rules simplifies training, aids compliance and understanding of critical safeguards, and helps transfer of experience and lessons learned. Effective industry wide implementation requires collaboration between operators, contractors, and subcontractors. To achieve the benefits of standardisation, all 9 Rules

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: subcontractors. To achieve the benefits of standardisation, all 9 Rules should be adopted as written and not be modified or substituted. It is accepted that operational risk profiles may differ, and the Rules may not address all an organisation’s fatality risks. In this case, companies are encouraged to manage these other risks through existing management systems or in other ways, e.g., campaigns,

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: through existing management systems or in other ways, e.g., campaigns, training, and workforce engagement, rather than creating additional Life-Saving Rules. It is important that the Rules are understood by all individuals, their supervisors, and their leaders, and that management have created the conditions necessary to enable everyone to follow the Rules. 3.1 Fundamental requirements Successful

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: enable everyone to follow the Rules. 3.1 Fundamental requirements Successful implementation of the Rules requires the following, as a minimum: • Organisations have an existing safety management system, containing the following supporting policies, processes and systems: – Worker Fitness for Duty including a drug and alcohol policy – Contractor (and subcontractor) Management program including bridging

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: alcohol policy – Contractor (and subcontractor) Management program including bridging arrangements, if applicable – Journey Management program – Safe systems of work including permit to work, and energy isolation – Management of change – Hazard identification and awareness, risk assessment and safeguard management – Field (self) verification providing checking and verification of critical tasks •

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: (self) verification providing checking and verification of critical tasks • A commitment that work does not start until all individuals involved are aware of and can confirm they can follow the Life-Saving Rules that are relevant to that work. • A requirement that work is not conducted without a pre-job risk assessment and a safety discussion, such as a toolbox talk, appropriate for the level of risk.

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: as a toolbox talk, appropriate for the level of risk. • Organisations define which procedures and equipment are safety critical and ensure impacted workers clearly understand what these are. • Personnel are trained and competent for the work they conduct. • Equipment is fit for purpose, properly maintained, and in working condition.

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: IOGP Life-Saving Rules • Before work starts, there are emergency response plans in place that have been developed from a review of potential emergency scenarios, which have suitable and sufficient resources available, and which are periodically drilled/tested. • Everyone is authorised to intervene or stop work without adverse consequences if they are in any doubt about the safety of an activity. •

text: in any doubt about the safety of an activity. • Suitable personal protective equipment is provided and worn in accordance with the requirements identified by the risk assessment and worksite policies. 3.2 Lessons learned in rules implementation Senior Management commitment is essential to successfully roll-out the Life- Saving Rules. The following steps for effective implementation are based on the

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: The following steps for effective implementation are based on the experience of IOGP member companies that have successfully implemented Life- Saving Rules equivalent programmes: • Conduct a risk assessment of your organisation’s activities and review historical data related to fatalities and high potential events within your own organisation (both company employee and contractors) and determine how

text: own organisation (both company employee and contractors) and determine how these align with the Life-Saving Rules. • Develop a business case/change management programme and discuss with leadership of both your organisation and your contractors and subcontractors to ensure commitment to implement the Life-Saving Rules. • Ensure implementation, use and compliance are owned by line-management (e.g. maintenance,

text: consultation with legal, supply chain and human resources departments). • Develop performance monitoring methods to determine the effective implementation and ongoing use of the Life-Saving Rules. • Use the IOGP Life-Saving Rules roll-out and engagement materials. Helping people follow the Rules Experience from member companies shows that the Life-Saving Rules, when consistently applied, prevent fatalities.

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: shows that the Life-Saving Rules, when consistently applied, prevent fatalities. Simply communicating the Rules and then holding people accountable for following them is not enough for effective implementation. To enable individuals to follow the Life-Saving Rules, organisations need first to provide the right conditions:

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: IOGP Life-Saving Rules • Everyone needs to know the Rules, understand their value, and what following the Rules means for their role. • The physical workplace conditions required to be able to follow the Rules need to present (e.g., certified anchor points provided for all work at height, vehicles equipped with seatbelts) • There need to be clear expectations set and supported from the top of the

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: clear expectations set and supported from the top of the organisation that work must not start unless the Rules can be followed, and these must be visible to the workforce, by, for example, ensuring physical workplace conditions are present. • Everyone must be given the authority and be encouraged to stop work and intervene if they observe a Life-Saving Rule (or indeed any other unsafe activity) actually,

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: a Life-Saving Rule (or indeed any other unsafe activity) actually, or potentially, not being followed. Proactive intervention may be the last opportunity to prevent injury or fatality. The focus on personal accountability for following the Rules is about care and concern for the individual and the well-being of everyone who works in our industry. If a Life-Saving Rule is not followed, organisations

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: our industry. If a Life-Saving Rule is not followed, organisations need to determine the reason to learn and improve workplace conditions, whether it resulted in undesirable consequences or not. Organisations have a role in positively reinforcing an open reporting culture, i.e. for self-reported errors and peer-to-peer interventions and responding appropriately where cases of ‘non-reporting’ are found.

section: IOGP Life-Saving Rules
text: interventions and responding appropriately where cases of ‘non-reporting’ are found. The intent is to understand what conditions and environment meant that a Rule was not followed, and drove people to do what they did, so that lessons can be identified, applied and learned. If a Life-Saving Rule is not followed, despite organisations providing all the necessary enabling conditions, then consequence

This might be relevant for the individual, or for those responsible for providing the enabling conditions. Of these, system-level issues were identified as causal in 90% of cases; these issues include unclear procedures (23%), capability and resources (30%) and mistakes due to labelling, alarms or tool issues (21%).

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: Process Safety Fundamentals Introduction The IOGP Process Safety Fundamentals (PSFs) were developed in 2020 based on an analysis of data reported by IOGP Members between 2007 and 2017 which showed that 128 people had lost their lives in 56 process safety events during this period. In response to this, the IOGP PSFs were developed as a resource to support companies to reduce, and ultimately eliminate,

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: a resource to support companies to reduce, and ultimately eliminate, fatal and high severity process safety events. As part of the update to this Report in 2026, the data analysis has been extended to include data up to and including 2024; within this period a further 30 PSE’s resulted in 47 people losing their lives. See Section 2 for more information on this updated analysis. Designed to support

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: for more information on this updated analysis. Designed to support those working in front-line operations, maintenance, and well related activities, the IOGP PSFs are informed by data and designed to draw attention to situations that are most likely to lead to process safety event fatalities. They are not intended to exhaustively address all process safety risks and hazards in the oil and gas industry,

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: safety risks and hazards in the oil and gas industry, but to be deployed in addition to a company’s existing systems for process safety management. IOGP PSFs are not intended to replace company policies, management systems, safe systems of work, safety training programmes, operating procedures, or work instructions; but to enhance them by reinforcing key aspects that have been identified as causal

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: by reinforcing key aspects that have been identified as causal (in the process safety event fatalities reported to IOGP). In this respect, the PSFs rely on suitable management systems being in place. Process safety is a disciplined framework for managing the hazards that have the potential to result in a major incident. Process safety is concerned with the integrity of operating systems and processes

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: is concerned with the integrity of operating systems and processes that handle hazardous substances and the hazards that arise from them. The content of the PSFs should be familiar to the industry, but defining the fundamentals (as presented in this Report) provides a clearer, more direct, focus for those working in roles which have influence on the management of process safety risk on the most important

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: the management of process safety risk on the most important aspects to be considered in their day-to-day activities. The roles which have an influence on process safety risk will include those who work in front-line operational or maintenance roles and technical personnel in roles which support the front-line (e.g., engineering support, technical authorities, project roles, etc.). Roles which influence

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: engineering support, technical authorities, project roles, etc.). Roles which influence process safety risk less directly (e.g., procurement, supply chain, planning, etc.) should also take notice of selected PSFs, as relevant to the scope of their involvement, and consider how these should be used to improve processes to manage risk. The PSFs do not replace any of the IOGP Life Saving Rules (LSRs):

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: not replace any of the IOGP Life Saving Rules (LSRs): they are intended as additional, complementary, recommendations. It is recommended that the PSFs are kept separate from the LSRs and not combined into a single list. The reason for this is that the LSRs are primarily focused on personal safety events, with some overlapping into process safety, whereas the PSFs are specifically targeted at the causes

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: safety, whereas the PSFs are specifically targeted at the causes of process safety events. Although there is overlap between some LSRs and PSFs (e.g., Energy Isolation/We Maintain Safe Isolation and Hot Work/We Control Ignition Sources), it was considered necessary to retain additional complementary information within the PSFs as these are identified causes of process safety events. Member company

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: these are identified causes of process safety events. Member company experience demonstrates that the PSFs and the LSRs can be used effectively in a complementary way.

IOGP is seeking industry standardization by recommending a core set of 10 PSFs relevant to all upstream operations. It is recognized, however, that some companies may wish to exchange a small number of the core set for others that are more tailored to their company’s specific

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis 2.1. Background The core set of PSFs were originally developed based on Process Safety Event (PSE) data reported by IOGP Member Companies over a period of eleven years (2007-2017). This data showed that 128 people lost their lives in 56 Process Safety Events. Analysis of the process safety related fatal incidents was conducted by a team of subject matter experts

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: incidents was conducted by a team of subject matter experts formed from the IOGP Process Safety Subcommittee (PSSC) with the aim of determining what types of Process Safety Fundamentals (PSF) were a factor in the incidents and how, if they had been implemented effectively, they might have prevented or mitigated the fatal consequences of these incidents. The analysis considered a broad range of potential

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: these incidents. The analysis considered a broad range of potential PSFs, influenced by both the information on the fatal incidents provided by IOGP Member Companies, and the team members’ experience. Each fatal PSE was reviewed and linked to one or more potential PSF. By determining which PSF could be linked to either the highest number of fatal incidents or number of fatalities allowed a shortlist

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: of fatal incidents or number of fatalities allowed a shortlist of PSF to be identified which eventually became the core set of 10 IOGP PSFs. This Report extends the analysis to include data reported by IOGP Member Companies for the years 2018–2024. All reported data, including cases where PSFs were already assigned to incidents (by the reporting Companies) in recent years has been reviewed and validated

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: reporting Companies) in recent years has been reviewed and validated by subject matter experts from the IOGP Process Safety Sub-Committee (PSSC). The results of this updated analysis are presented in the following Sections. 2.2. Fatal Tier 1 PSE To update this analysis, data for PSE involving fatalities during the years 2018-2024 were added to the original dataset2. The extended dataset shows that

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis
text: added to the original dataset2. The extended dataset shows that 175 people lost their lives in 86 PSEs over the 18-year period 2007-2024. IOGP Member Companies provided sufficient detail in 72 of the 86 incident reports to allow a reasonable assessment linking each event to one or more specific PSFs. As shown in Figure 1, 94% of these fatal PSEs (68 out of 72 incidents) could be associated with one

section: 2. Process Safety Event Data Analysis

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: Process Safety Fundamentals 5. Definitions Key steps in operation or maintenance procedure – A procedure step, series of steps, or action that, if performed improperly, will cause irreversible harm to plant, equipment, or people or will significantly impact plant operation. It is also known as “critical steps”. Safe isolation – The separation of plant and equipment from every source of energy (pressure,

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: of plant and equipment from every source of energy (pressure, electrical, and mechanical) in such a way that the separation is secure. Non- proven isolation methods (i.e., without provision to confirm effectiveness of the isolation) should not be considered a safe isolation when dealing with hazardous conditions (e.g., hazardous substances, pressure, temperature, etc.). Hazardous material – Materials

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: (e.g., hazardous substances, pressure, temperature, etc.). Hazardous material – Materials that can cause harm, for example by igniting or being toxic. API 754 and IOGP Report 456 - Process safety - recommended practice on key performance indicators refer to the United Nations Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods. Like-for-like equipment change – changes that are a “replacement in kind”

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: equipment change – changes that are a “replacement in kind” which means to replace with the same design, same rating, same materials of construction, etc. Safe Operating Limit (SOL) – Limits established for process parameters, such as temperature, pressure, level, flow, or concentration, based on a combination of equipment design limits and the dynamics of the process. For further reading refer to

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: the dynamics of the process. For further reading refer to IOGP Report 456. Walk the line – Walk the line is a practice sharing programme that provides a variety of tools to help ensure that operators know where energy will flow between two points in a process. Typical activities for walk the line to be applied: • Return to operation after maintenance or turnaround. • Changeover of equipment (e.g.,

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: operation after maintenance or turnaround. • Changeover of equipment (e.g., relief valves, filters, pumps, compressors). • Transfer of fluids (e.g., loading operations). • Sequential or batch operations (e.g., pigging, bed regeneration). • Temporary pipework. Hardware Barrier – Primary containment, process equipment and engineered systems designed and managed to prevent Loss of Primary Containment

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: systems designed and managed to prevent Loss of Primary Containment (LOPC) and other types of asset integrity or process safety events, and mitigate any potential consequences of such events. These are checked and maintained by people (in critical activity/tasks). For further reading refer to IOGP Report 544 - Standardization of barrier definitions. Human Barriers – Barriers that rely on the actions

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: definitions. Human Barriers – Barriers that rely on the actions of people capable of carrying out activities designed to prevent LOPC and other types of asset integrity or process safety events and mitigate any potential consequences of such events. For further reading refer to IOGP Report 544.

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: Process Safety Fundamentals Weak signals – Weak signals are ‘tell-tale” signs, which are not considered normal operating conditions of a given plant (unusual noise or vibration; pressure or level readings that are not as expected, etc.). There are various methods to identify and report “weak signals” such as operator rounds, near miss programmes, etc. A constant status of alertness to weak signals,

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: programmes, etc. A constant status of alertness to weak signals, such as asking the right questions and picking up on signals of potential failure when on-site is a key behaviour for safety leaders at every level in the organization to help reduce the risk of incidents. Risk normalization – The tendency to underestimate a risk that has become familiar and is associated with tasks that we undertake

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: become familiar and is associated with tasks that we undertake regularly without incident. If someone deviates from safe practices on one occasion, it increases the likelihood this behaviour will be repeated, until this unsafe behaviour becomes routine and accepted. This gradual justification and acceptance of unsafe behaviour can happen to any individual or organization and vigilance is required

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: happen to any individual or organization and vigilance is required to ensure that established safe practice is maintained. Hazardous Area Classification (HAC) – Any place an ignitable concentration of flammable gases or vapours may occur in quantities that would require special precautions to protect the safety of workers and plant. In this context, ‘special precautions’ are best taken as relating

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: In this context, ‘special precautions’ are best taken as relating to the construction, installation, and use of apparatus. It should be noted there is limitation with HAC, whereby migration of flammable material (gas dispersion) can occur beyond limits of HAC. Abnormal situation – An abnormal situation is a disturbance or series of disturbances in a process that causes plant operations to deviate

section: Process Safety Fundamentals
text: disturbances in a process that causes plant operations to deviate from their normal operating state (for further reading on normal operating limits refer to IOGP Report 456 – Process safety – recommended practice on key performance indicators). The disturbances may be minimal or catastrophic, and may cause production losses or, in serious cases, endanger human life. Up-to-date P&IDs – Updated set

text: serious cases, endanger human life. Up-to-date P&IDs – Updated set of drawings Piping and Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID) reflecting the current and real plant status. Usually submitted by a contractor upon completion of a construction project and used in the operations phase. Depending on the plant status these can also be known as Red-Line Mark-Up or As-Built P&IDs.

The basket was guided into a load handling arrangement consisting of rails, which limit the movement horizontally, and three manually-operated hatches. WHAT WENT WRONG: The incident was triggered by nitrogen

Without airflow, oxygen was

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports

Without airflow, oxygen was gradually displaced overnight creating a hazardous atmosphere that posed a serious risk of unconsciousness and fatality. section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed. WHAT WENT WRONG: The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with no effective barrier against dropped objects. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: below with no effective barrier against dropped objects. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS: All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier (e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally

section: Safety performance indicators – 2025 data: High potential event reports
text: nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project- wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.
